props.title: High Wall

sections.content: High Wall stands as a prime example of psychological film noir, blending criminal justice themes with emerging post-war interest in mental health treatment. Robert Taylor delivers a haunting performance as Steven Kenet, a traumatized war veteran accused of murder who can't remember if he's guilty. The film shares thematic DNA with Spellbound (1945) and The Dark Past (1948), exploring memory loss and psychoanalysis through a noir lens. Director Curtis Bernhardt, who also helmed Possessed (1947), brings his signature German Expressionist influences to create claustrophobic asylum scenes and shadowy interrogations. movies.title: High Wall
movies.slug: A war veteran with memory loss must prove his innocence with help from a psychiatrist

sections.content: The film's exploration of PTSD and mental trauma reflects Hollywood's growing fascination with psychiatry in the late 1940s. Like The Snake Pit (1948) and Shock Corridor (1963), High Wall uses mental institution settings to create both tension and social commentary. Audrey Totter's portrayal of Dr. Ann Lorrison marks a departure from typical noir femme fatales, presenting instead a professional woman whose scientific approach to mental health challenges the era's more sensationalistic treatments. SUBHEAD: Post-War Psychological Noir

High Wall fits into a specific subset of post-WWII noir films dealing with veteran readjustment and psychological trauma. Similar themes appear in Somewhere in the Night (1946) and The Blue Dahlia (1946), where returning soldiers grapple with memory loss and suspected crimes. The film's use of experimental treatments like sodium pentothal reflects actual post-war psychiatric practices, while its visual style - particularly the asylum sequences - draws heavily from German Expressionism, much like The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920).
